newsitem.title: USA: St. Louis airport expansion seen as vital.
newsitem.headline: St. Louis airport expansion seen as vital.

text.p: If there is one thing that most political and business leaders in the St. Louis region agree on it is that Lambert-St. Louis International Airport must be expanded.
Without the expansion, the St. Louis area "becomes third rate in the morning," said Earle Harbison, former president of Monsanto Co.
Expanding the airport, according to Buzz Westfall, St. Louis County Executive, is critical to the region's "economic vitality" going into the 21st Century.

"I think it's extremely important," said Andy Craig, chairman and chief executive officer of Boatmen's Bancshares Inc. "Probably the most important event for the economic future of the area to happen for some time."
Business and political leaders have formed an alliance to push for the expansion.

They cite a variety of statistics to back their claim for the need. Lambert was the second fastest growing airport in the world in 1995 behind Seoul, Korea. That same year, the airport had the dubious distinction of having the second worst record for delays.

Those delays are costing airlines, particularly Lambert hub airline TWA, $70 million a year, according to Richard C.D. Fleming, president and chief executive officer of the St. Louis Regional Commerce and Growth Association, a business organization.

According to the group, the expansion would triple the airport's economic impact to $15 billion over the next 15 years. The airport's expansion, which has been in the works for several years, cleared a major hurdle in September when Federal Aviation Administration released a draft environmental impact statement.

The $1.88 billion so-called W-1W plan calls for a new 9,000 foot-long parallel runway that would allow for airline operations during inclement weather. The plan also includes expansion of the terminal and road improvements.
St. Louis plans to finance the project largely with general airport revenue bonds and possibly with bonds backed by passenger facility charges.

FAA's comment period for the plan was extended to Jan 17, according to Mike Faltermeier, manager of planning and programming for the FAA's airports division's central region. After reviewing the comments, the next step for the agency would be a final environmental impact statement, followed in about 30 days by a record of decision, Faltermeier added.
But expanding the airport has not been without problems.

"One of the most interesting things about this is it's not like we're building a brand new airport on green space. We're building an airport at an existing airport and it makes it somewhat difficult," St. Louis Mayor Freeman Bosley Jr. said.

To expand the airport, located about 17 miles from St. Louis, the city needs land. And Bridgeton Mayor Conrad Bowers, who stands to lose a large chunk of his 17-square-mile, home-rule suburb of 18,000 residents to the project, is fighting the city.
"It would destroy our city," he contended, adding that St. Louis is "trying to shoe-horn in a runway that will not fit."
Nearly 2,000 residential properties, mainly in Bridgeton, would have to be purchased and razed to accommodate that runway, according to the FAA draft report.

"Bridgeton will do what is necessary to protect the city of Bridgeton from unwise airport expansion," Bowers said, adding that better and cheaper options exist to allow for greater capacity at Lambert.

Still, Bridgeton's first legal volley against the expansion plan was dismissed last week by a Missouri circuit court judge, who ruled the city's lawsuit, which centered on zoning issues, was premature because the airport plan had not received FAA approval.
Bowers vowed to continue the legal fight against the W-1W plan, adding that he was gaining support from other communities near Lambert.
